assets.alt: spatial relationship of human trilaminar disc
assets.caption: An original schematic of the three germ layers in a representative region of the early human embryonic disc. Ectoderm faces the amniotic side, mesoderm lies between, and definitive endoderm faces the yolk-sac side. During gastrulation, epiblast cells give rise to these three layers; this still image does not show that movement. Colours, cell shapes and layer thicknesses are simplified.
assets.equivalentExplanation: A shallow human embryonic disc contains three cellular sheets: blue ectoderm above, coral mesoderm between, and gold definitive endoderm below. The upper face is toward the amniotic space; the lower face is toward the yolk-sac space. Epiblast cells form all three germ layers during gastrulation. This representative still image shows the resulting layer arrangement, not cell migration or complete embryo anatomy.

assets.alt: Spatial recognition of uterine tubes, open fimbrial ends, endometrial lining and continuous uterine-cervical-vaginal route
assets.caption: An original frontal schematic of the internal reproductive tract. The open fimbrial end of each uterine tube lies near an ovary; it is not sealed to the ovarian surface. The tubes enter the uterus above its inner endometrial lining. The uterine cavity continues through the cervical canal into the vagina. The pale supporting bands between ovaries and uterus are ligaments, not an oocyte route. Relative size and cavity width are simplified.
assets.equivalentExplanation: Two ovaries lie beside the open fimbrial ends of the uterine tubes. There is a gap between each ovary and tube. Each tube enters the upper uterus; its cavity continues downward through the cervix into the vagina. Endometrium is the inner uterine lining, distinct from the thicker muscle wall. The pale supporting bands are ligaments and do not carry the oocyte. This frontal view is schematic and does not show external genital anatomy.

assets.alt: Anatomical recognition of sperm transport and accessory-gland junctions
assets.caption: Original schematic side view of one side of the paired reproductive pathway. Small ducts connect the testis to the epididymal head; its coiled body leads to a lower tail that continues into the vas deferens. The vas joins the seminal-vesicle duct to form an ejaculatory duct entering the urethra within the prostate. A bulbourethral duct joins below. The urethra opens through the penis. The pale bladder is a landmark: sperm do not enter its cavity. Ducts are separated for visibility; their projected crossing is not a junction, and proportions and fine tissue detail are simplified.
assets.equivalentExplanation: Trace the continuous route from the testis through small ducts into the epididymal head, along its body to its lower tail, then up the vas deferens. A seminal-vesicle duct joins the vas to form an ejaculatory duct. That duct opens into the urethra within the prostate; a bulbourethral duct enters the urethra below. The urethra continues through the penis to the exterior. The bladder cavity is separate from sperm transport, and a projected crossing of drawn ducts is not a junction.

assets.alt: Distinguish germ cells, tubule support and interstitial hormone release
assets.caption: Within a testis, germ cells develop among Sertoli supporting cells in a seminiferous tubule. Interstitial cells between tubules release testosterone into blood. A hormone measurement does not establish complete sperm development.
assets.equivalentExplanation: The round inset is a seminiferous tubule, not the whole testis. Germ cells develop among Sertoli supporting cells inside it. The open central lumen receives later sperm stages. Interstitial cells lie outside the tubule and release testosterone into a nearby blood vessel. These locations separate sperm development, cellular support and hormone secretion.

assets.alt: Section of a placenta showing maternal blood around branching villi and fetal capillaries inside them, connected to the umbilical vessels.
assets.caption: Maternal blood surrounds chorionic villi while fetal blood remains inside their capillaries. The two blood supplies are separated by tissue; gas diffusion and other selective transport processes allow exchange. Supplied Biology textbook, Chapter15, p.517, Figure15.11A, MHR.
assets.equivalentExplanation: Chorionic villi are branching projections of placental tissue. Fetal capillaries are small blood vessels inside these projections; maternal blood occupies spaces around them. Tissue separates the two blood supplies. Umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placenta. The umbilical vein returns blood toward the fetus. Oxygen commonly moves toward fetal blood and carbon dioxide toward maternal blood; other substances use different selective transfer processes. Blood-vessel direction and the exchange boundary matter more than red or blue colouring. The placenta is not an absolute filter against harmful exposures.
assets.provenance: supplied textbook; restricted local blocked-review use; public redistribution and export are not cleared.

scienceReview.finding: Fetal umbilical vessels lead to capillaries within villi; maternal vessels open to blood spaces outside the fetal capillaries. Inset distinguishes fetal and maternal portions and shows their boundary; no direct merged maternal/fetal blood tube is drawn. Labels for uterus, placenta, cord and amniotic fluid are readable at native extraction size. Use an authored equivalent to explain directional names: umbilical arteries carry blood away from the fetus; the umbilical vein carries blood toward it. Colour is illustrative and cannot replace direction labels. This is a section through a complex branching interface, not a complete vessel count or to-scale reconstruction. Original caption oversimplifies all nutrient transfer as diffusion; it is excluded. Adjacent teaching must distinguish gas diffusion from other selective transport processes.

assets.alt: A loop connects cervical stretch, oxytocin release and uterine contraction, with delivery as its endpoint.
assets.caption: Original schematic. Oxytocin supports contractions that can reinforce cervical stretch during labour. Delivery removes the main stretch stimulus.
assets.equivalentExplanation: Cervical stretch during labour sends sensory signals associated with oxytocin release. Hypothalamic neurons make oxytocin; it is stored and released through the posterior pituitary into blood. Responsive uterine tissue contracts, which can increase cervical stretch and reinforce this loop. Delivery removes the main stretch stimulus. This is one mechanism within labour; it does not claim that fetal size alone starts labour or that the loop explains all timing and tissue responses.

assets.alt: Parallel pathways distinguish prolactin-supported milk synthesis from oxytocin-supported milk ejection.
assets.caption: Original schematic. Milk-producing cells and contractile supporting cells have different responses: making milk and moving existing milk.
assets.equivalentExplanation: Suckling provides sensory input supporting both pathways. Anterior-pituitary prolactin supports milk synthesis by milk-producing cells. Oxytocin, made in hypothalamic neurons and released through posterior pituitary, supports contraction of myoepithelial cells around secretory tissue, helping eject existing milk. After placental delivery, falling steroid levels support greater synthesis; prolactin is not first created only after birth. Synthesis, ejection and effective transfer are related but distinct outcomes.

assets.alt: Two parental sets establish the diploid zygote
assets.caption: Two parental sets establish the diploid zygote.

assets.alt: Locate fertilization, transfer and implantation
assets.caption: Locate fertilization, transfer and implantation.

assets.alt: Trace early hCG support through its actual targets
assets.caption: Trace early hCG support through its actual targets.
